lessons.meaning: any ~ at all / no matter which
lessons.example_en: I eat anything well.
lessons.note: **이든지** after a consonant, **든지** after a vowel: 언제든지, 누구든지, 뭐든지. It says the choice does not matter — any one is fine.

sentences.english: Come anytime.
Anyone can come.
Ask me anything.
Any food is fine with me.
Anywhere is fine.

lessons.meaning: shows another person's feeling (turns a feeling adjective into a verb)
lessons.example_en: My little brother is scared of the puppy.
lessons.note: Feeling adjectives like 좋다, 싫다, 무섭다 describe **my own** feelings. To describe **another person's** feelings, add **-아/어하다**: 좋아하다, 싫어하다, 무서워하다. The thing felt then takes 을/를.

sentences.english: My friend likes Korean food.
My younger sibling hates vegetables.
The child is scared of dogs.
My younger sibling was happy to get the present.
My friend finds Korean difficult.

lessons.meaning: I'm thinking of (doing) — a loose, tentative plan
lessons.example_en: I'm thinking of going to the sea this weekend.
lessons.note: **-(으)ㄹ까 하다** expresses a plan you are still considering: **-ㄹ까 하다** after a vowel stem (가다 → 갈까 해요), **-을까 하다** after a consonant (먹다 → 먹을까 해요). It is weaker than -(으)려고 하다.

sentences.english: I'm thinking of resting at home this weekend.
I'm thinking of learning Korean cooking.
I'm thinking of eating bibimbap for lunch.
I'm thinking of moving next month.
I'm thinking of taking a walk in the park.

lessons.meaning: casual speech ending (with close friends)
lessons.example_en: I'm going home now.
lessons.note: Drop the **요** from the polite -아/어요 form to get casual speech: 가요 → 가, 먹어요 → 먹어, 해요 → 해. Use it only with close friends, children, or people younger than you.

sentences.english: What are you doing now?
I'm eating lunch with a friend.
I'm going home now.
The weather is really nice today.
Call me later.

lessons.meaning: casual 'to be' (am / is / are, between friends)
lessons.example_en: This is my bag.
lessons.note: The casual form of 이에요/예요: **이야** after a consonant (학생이야), **야** after a vowel (가수야). The negative is 아니야. Use it only with close friends.

sentences.english: This is my book.
That person is my younger sibling.
Today is my birthday.
My friend is a singer.
Is this your umbrella?

lessons.meaning: whether (to) — an undecided question inside a sentence
lessons.example_en: I haven't decided yet what to eat.
lessons.note: **-(으)ㄹ지** embeds an undecided question, often before 정하다, 생각하다, 고민하다: 갈지, 먹을지, 뭘 살지. Use **-ㄹ지** after a vowel stem and **-을지** after a consonant.

sentences.english: I haven't decided what to buy yet.
I'm thinking about where to go on a trip.
I'm worried about what to wear tomorrow.
We are deciding what to eat for dinner.
I don't know yet when I will depart.

lessons.meaning: having done ~ / because ~ (spoken alternative to -아/어서)
lessons.example_en: I saved up money and went on a trip.
lessons.note: **-아/어 가지고** links an action or reason to what follows, like -아/어서 but more colloquial: 사 가지고 (having bought it), 늦어 가지고 (because I was late).

sentences.english: I bought fruit and went to my friend's house.
sentences.korean: 과일을 사 가지고 친구 집에 갔어요.
accepted: 과일을 사 가지고 친구 집에 갔어요.
과일을 사 가지고 친구 집에 갔습니다.

sentences.english: I got up late, so I couldn't eat breakfast.
sentences.korean: 늦게 일어나 가지고 아침을 못 먹었어요.
accepted: 늦게 일어나 가지고 아침을 못 먹었어요.
늦게 일어나 가지고 아침을 못 먹었습니다.

sentences.english: I made kimbap and ate it together with my friends.
sentences.korean: 김밥을 만들어 가지고 친구들하고 같이 먹었어요.
accepted: 김밥을 만들어 가지고 친구들하고 같이 먹었어요.
김밥을 만들어 가지고 친구들과 같이 먹었어요.

sentences.english: It was so cold that I caught a cold.
sentences.korean: 날씨가 너무 추워 가지고 감기에 걸렸어요.
accepted: 날씨가 너무 추워 가지고 감기에 걸렸어요.

sentences.english: I earned money and bought a new phone.
sentences.korean: 돈을 벌어 가지고 새 휴대폰을 샀어요.
accepted: 돈을 벌어 가지고 새 휴대폰을 샀어요.
돈을 벌어 가지고 새 핸드폰을 샀어요.

lessons.meaning: to know / not know whether (where, what, why...)
lessons.example_en: Do you know where the bank is?
lessons.note: **-는지** turns a question into a clause before 알다/모르다: 어디에 있는지, 뭘 좋아하는지. With adjectives and 이다 use **-(으)ㄴ지** (얼마나 큰지, 무슨 뜻인지), and add 왜/누가/어디 for question words.

sentences.english: Do you know where the subway station is?
I don't know what this word means.
Do you know what time the store opens?
sentences.korean: 가게가 몇 시에 문을 여는지 알아요?
accepted: 가게가 몇 시에 문을 여는지 알아요?

sentences.english: I don't know why my friend isn't coming.
I know what food my friend likes.

lessons.meaning: if you intend to / in order to (you should...)
lessons.example_en: If you want to buy a ticket, go early.
lessons.note: **-(으)려면** means 'if you plan to do X': **-려면** after a vowel stem, **-으려면** after a consonant. The second clause usually gives advice or a requirement, with -(으)세요 or -아/어야 해요.

sentences.english: If you want to speak Korean well, practice every day.
If you want to go to Busan, take the train.
If you want to become healthy, exercise often.
If you want to arrive by 9, you have to leave now.
accepted: 아홉 시까지 도착하려면 지금 출발해야 해요.

sentences.english: If you want to borrow a book, you need a library card.
accepted: 책을 빌리려면 도서관 카드가 있어야 해요.

lessons.meaning: did ~ and then (a finished action followed by a change)
lessons.example_en: I opened the door and then closed it again.
lessons.note: **-았/었다가** marks a completed action followed by a change — often the opposite action: 갔다가 왔어요, 샀다가 바꿨어요. Both actions share the same subject.

sentences.english: I went to the market and came back.
I turned on the light and then turned it off.
I bought the clothes and then exchanged them.
I stood up and then sat down again.
I put on my coat and then took it off because it was hot.

lessons.meaning: soft, polite question ending
lessons.example_en: Do you have time now?
lessons.note: **-나요?** asks a question more softly than -아/어요?: attach it to a verb stem (가나요?, 먹나요?, 있나요?). With adjectives, **-(으)ㄴ가요?** is common instead (큰가요?).

sentences.english: Does this bus go to City Hall?
Do you have time this weekend?
What time does the movie start?
Do you often eat Korean food?
Is it raining outside now?

lessons.meaning: about / concerning
lessons.example_en: I am learning about Korean culture.
lessons.note: **에 대해서** (= 에 대해) marks the topic something is about: 역사에 대해서 이야기해요. Before a noun, use **에 대한** instead: 한국에 대한 책.

sentences.english: We talked about the trip.
I want to know about Korean history.
The teacher explained about the exam.
I am writing about my family.
Please think about this problem.

lessons.meaning: I'm not sure whether / I wonder if
lessons.example_en: I'm not sure whether it will rain tomorrow.
lessons.note: **-(으)ㄹ지 모르겠다** expresses uncertainty about the future or an unknown: 갈 수 있을지 모르겠어요. Use **-ㄹ지** after a vowel stem and **-을지** after a consonant.

sentences.english: I'm not sure whether I can finish this work today.
sentences.korean: 오늘 이 일을 다 할 수 있을지 모르겠어요.
accepted: 오늘 이 일을 다 할 수 있을지 모르겠어요.
오늘 이 일을 끝낼 수 있을지 모르겠어요.

sentences.english: I'm not sure if the weather will be good tomorrow.
I'm not sure whether my friend will like this present.
accepted: 친구가 이 선물을 마음에 들어 할지 모르겠어요.

sentences.english: I don't know if I'll be able to get up early tomorrow.
sentences.korean: 내일 일찍 일어날 수 있을지 모르겠어요.
accepted: 내일 일찍 일어날 수 있을지 모르겠어요.

sentences.english: I'm not sure whether there will be seats.

lessons.meaning: compared to
lessons.example_en: Compared to last year, the weather is warm.
lessons.note: **에 비해서** (= 에 비해) compares something against a standard: 값에 비해서 좋아요 (good for the price). It is similar to 보다 but a little more formal.

sentences.english: This restaurant is cheap compared to other restaurants.
sentences.korean: 이 식당은 다른 식당에 비해서 싸요.
accepted: 이 식당은 다른 식당에 비해서 싸요.
이 식당은 다른 식당에 비해 싸요.

sentences.english: Compared to last week, I'm busy this week.
Compared to the city, the countryside is quiet.
Compared to my younger sibling, I am tall.
Compared to yesterday, today is cold.

lessons.meaning: reported question (someone asked whether...)
lessons.example_en: My friend asked where I was going.
lessons.note: To report a question, attach **-냐고 하다/묻다** to the stem: 가냐고, 먹냐고, 바쁘냐고. In everyday spoken Korean plain **-냐고** works for verbs and adjectives alike, and 물어봤어요 is common for 'asked'.

sentences.english: My friend asked whether I'm busy today.
The teacher asked where I live.
My mother asked whether I had eaten.
My friend asked whether the movie was fun.
My friend asked when I'm coming.

lessons.meaning: reported command (someone told me to...)
lessons.example_en: The doctor told me to rest well.
lessons.note: To report a command, attach **-라고 하다** to a vowel stem and **-으라고 하다** to a consonant stem: 가라고, 읽으라고, 쉬라고. For 'told me not to', use **-지 말라고 하다**.

sentences.english: The teacher told us to read the book.
My mother told me to get up early.
The doctor told me to take the medicine.
My friend told me to come quickly.
The teacher told us not to be late.

lessons.meaning: as soon as / just as
lessons.example_en: I'll call you as soon as I arrive home.
lessons.note: **-는 대로** after a verb stem means 'as soon as' (도착하는 대로) or 'just as' (제가 하는 대로 하세요). For a past action, **-(으)ㄴ 대로** means 'as it was done': 들은 대로.

sentences.english: I'll call you as soon as work ends.
Please do as I do.
As soon as I get home, I'll send the photos.
Please write it just as you heard it.
As soon as spring comes, I want to go on a trip.
sentences.korean: 봄이 오는 대로 여행을 가고 싶어요.
accepted: 봄이 오는 대로 여행을 가고 싶어요.
봄이 오는 대로 여행을 하고 싶어요.

lessons.meaning: reported request for oneself (asked someone to do ~ for them)
lessons.example_en: My friend asked me to take a photo for them.
lessons.note: When reporting '-아/어 주세요' said for the speaker's own benefit, use **-아/어 달라고 하다**: 도와 달라고 했어요. If the favor was for a third person, use -아/어 주라고 하다 instead.

sentences.english: My friend asked me to help.
My younger sibling asked me to buy ice cream.
My friend asked me to lend them a book.
The student asked the teacher to explain again.
sentences.korean: 학생이 선생님께 다시 설명해 달라고 했어요.
accepted: 학생이 선생님께 다시 설명해 달라고 했어요.
학생이 선생님에게 다시 설명해 달라고 했어요.

sentences.english: My mother asked me to open the window.

lessons.meaning: onto / into / on (the spot where something is put)
lessons.example_en: Write your name here.
lessons.note: **에다가** (often shortened to **에다**) marks the spot where something is put, written, or added: 벽에다가 걸어요, 가방에다가 넣었어요. It is a colloquial, emphatic 에.

sentences.english: Please write your name here.
I put my wallet into my bag.
I hung the picture on the wall.
Please put the box on the desk.
I planted flowers in the yard.

lessons.meaning: don't do ~, (do ... instead)
lessons.example_en: Don't take the bus; take the subway.
lessons.note: **-지 말고** rejects one action and suggests another: A하지 말고 B하세요. It comes from -지 말다. With nouns, use **말고** alone: 커피 말고 차 주세요.

sentences.english: Don't watch TV; read a book.
Don't worry; try calling your friend.
Let's not eat out; let's eat at home.
Don't take a taxi; walk.
Don't just sit; exercise.

lessons.meaning: any ~ at all / nobody (with a negative)
lessons.example_en: Anything is fine.
lessons.note: **아무 + 나** means 'any at all': 아무거나, 아무 때나, 아무나. With a negative verb, **아무도** means 'nobody' and **아무것도** means 'nothing': 교실에 아무도 없어요.

sentences.english: Anything is fine.
There is nobody in the classroom.
I didn't eat anything this morning.
Come by anytime.
Anyone can do this work.
sentences.korean: 이 일은 아무나 할 수 있어요.
accepted: 이 일은 아무나 할 수 있어요.

lessons.meaning: nothing but / only (always with a negative verb)
lessons.example_en: I have only a thousand won.
lessons.note: **밖에** means 'only' and must pair with a negative: 조금밖에 없어요, 한 명밖에 안 왔어요. Compare **만**, which takes a positive verb.

sentences.english: I have only a little money.
Only one student came.
I slept only three hours.
There is only one apple left.
I know only a few Korean words.

lessons.meaning: that (I) did before — completed past modifier
lessons.example: 작년에 갔던 식당에 또 가고 싶어요.
lessons.example_en: I want to go again to the restaurant I went to last year.
lessons.note: **-았/었던** modifies a noun with a finished past event you recall: 먹었던 음식, 만났던 사람. It stresses that the action is completely over, unlike -던, which suggests a habit or something unfinished.

sentences.english: The movie I watched last week was fun.
This is a book I read when I was young.
Let's go again to the cafe we went to last time.
The food I ate in Busan was delicious.
I met the friend I had met last year again.

lessons.meaning: that (I) used to / was doing — recollected modifier
lessons.example_en: It's a song I used to sing often as a child.
lessons.note: **-던** modifies a noun with a past habit or an unfinished action: 다니던 학교 (the school I used to attend), 마시던 커피 (the coffee I was drinking).

sentences.english: This is the school I used to attend.
Where is the coffee I was drinking?
I found the book I was reading.
This is a song I used to listen to often.
I passed by the house I used to live in.

lessons.meaning: as much as / to the same degree as
lessons.example_en: The younger brother is as tall as the older brother.
lessons.note: **만큼** attaches to a noun to say two things are equal in degree: 저만큼, 어제만큼. After a verb, use -(으)ㄹ 만큼 (to the extent that).

sentences.english: Today is as hot as summer.
My friend speaks Korean as well as a Korean person.
accepted: 제 친구는 한국 사람만큼 한국어를 잘해요.

sentences.english: This bag is as expensive as that bag.
My younger sibling eats as much as me.
Today it rained as much as yesterday.

lessons.meaning: I noticed that ~ (recalling a personal discovery)
lessons.example_en: I found that restaurant's food really delicious.
lessons.note: **-더군요** reports something you personally observed in the past, with mild surprise: 춥더군요, 잘하더군요. Add 았/었 for an event already completed when you noticed it: 벌써 갔더군요.

sentences.english: I noticed the department store was really crowded.
I found the weather in Busan warm.
I saw that that singer sings really well.
The movie was more fun than I expected.
I found the new cafe quiet.

lessons.meaning: to (mistakenly) think that / to not know that
lessons.example_en: I thought it was raining today.
lessons.note: **-는 줄 알았다** often means 'I wrongly thought...': 자는 줄 알았어요. **-는 줄 몰랐다** means 'I didn't know...'. With adjectives and 이다 use -(으)ㄴ/인 줄, and for the future -(으)ㄹ 줄.

sentences.english: I thought today was Saturday.
I thought you were sleeping.
I didn't know you spoke Korean so well.
I thought it was raining outside.
I didn't know the exam was today.

lessons.meaning: thanks to
lessons.example_en: Thanks to my teacher, I did well on the exam.
lessons.note: **덕분에** credits a good result to someone or something: 친구 덕분에. After a verb, use -(으)ㄴ 덕분에: 도와준 덕분에. For bad results, use 때문에 instead.

sentences.english: Thanks to my friend, I found the way easily.
Thanks to the good weather, the trip was enjoyable.
Thanks to your help, I finished the work early.
Thanks to my parents, I was able to study in Korea.
sentences.korean: 부모님 덕분에 한국에서 공부할 수 있었어요.
accepted: 부모님 덕분에 한국에서 공부할 수 있었어요.
부모님 덕분에 한국에서 공부할 수 있었습니다.

sentences.english: Thanks to the medicine, I feel much better now.
